opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I used to believe it pretty firmly, and the reasoning felt airtight at the time. AI research seemed like the most open-ended kind of work there is. You're not executing a well-defined task. You're deciding which problems are worth working on, forming hypotheses with very little evidence, designing experiments, and then reading messy results and figuring out what they actually mean. A lot of that runs on taste and intuition built up over years of failed experiments. I thought that kind of judgment would be the hardest thing for a model to acquire, because there's no clean dataset of "good research taste" to train on.

There was also a more self-referential argument. If AI is the thing that automates everything else, then the people building AI are the last link in the chain. You'd need humans to push the frontier until the very end, almost by definition.

But my view has shifted quite a bit, mostly from watching how my own daily work has changed. When I break down what I actually spend my time on, a huge fraction isn't the brilliant-insight part. It's writing training code, debugging, running ablations, babysitting jobs, reading logs, making plots, skimming papers to check whether someone already tried an idea. Those pieces turn out to be very automatable, and coding agents are already doing a lot of them better and faster than I would. And once the execution loop gets cheap, the bottleneck shifts. You can run ten times more experiments, and the models start to show something that looks like taste, because they've seen so many research trajectories.

AI research also has a property most fields don't: the feedback loop is fast and mostly digital. You don't need a wet lab or a factory. You change some code, train, get a number back. That's exactly the kind of environment where automation advances fastest. So instead of being the last job to go, it might be one of the first places where AI substantially takes over, and the labs have every incentive to make that happen, since automating their own research is the most direct way to speed up progress.

So now I'd put it differently. The role of the human researcher is changing rather than disappearing overnight. Less time doing the work, more time deciding what's worth doing and judging whether the results really mean what they seem to. But I no longer feel confident that even that last layer is safe for very long.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI researchers once seemed like the last link in the chain, but does not state that AI would become uncontrollable if it could conduct AI research.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started as a kind of joke among us in the lab, but the more I thought about it, the more I believed it.

The logic goes like this. Think about what it would actually mean for AI to replace an AI researcher. It would mean the system can do the whole loop itself: look at where the field is stuck, come up with a genuinely new idea, design the experiment, run it, read the results, and then figure out what the results are telling you that you didn't expect. That last part is the hard one. Most of research is not the moment when the idea works. It's the weeks when nothing works and you have to decide whether your idea is wrong or your code is wrong or your evaluation is measuring the wrong thing.

So if a model can do that reliably, that is basically a model that can improve itself. And once you have that, you don't really have "jobs" in the normal sense anymore. The question of who gets replaced stops being interesting, because everything changes at once. That's why I said we'd be last. Not because we're special or smarter than, say, a radiologist. It's that our job is the one that sits closest to the thing itself. Replacing us is the finish line, not a step along the way.

I'll admit I've become less confident recently. A lot of what I do day to day is not the heroic part. It's writing data loaders, chasing a bug in distributed training, rerunning a sweep because I forgot a flag. Those pieces are already getting eaten. Maybe half of my actual hours. So the honest version is: the role of "AI researcher" might survive to the end, but the person doing it in 2030 will spend their day very differently than I do now. More taste, more judgment about which questions matter, much less typing.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI that could conduct research would be able to improve itself and that everything would change at once, but it does not state that AI would become uncontrollable.

astra-6.text:
My intuition was that AI researchers are working on the boundary of what AI can do. In many other jobs, you can define the task and train a system to perform it. Research is harder to pin down: you have to decide what question matters, figure out why an approach failed, and sometimes change the problem entirely.

So I thought AI would automate more and more of our tools before it could automate that whole process. But there’s a weakness in that argument: being the people who build AI doesn’t make us immune to it. If AI becomes good at proposing ideas, running experiments, and judging the results, then a lot of AI research could be automated too. The key question is whether it can choose productive research directions, not just execute experiments.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI automating research and choosing research directions, but does not say that AI would become uncontrollable.

sol-6.1.text:
I thought AI research would be one of the last jobs to be automated because researchers are building the systems doing the automating. It seemed like you’d still need people to decide what to investigate, recognize a promising result, and figure out why an experiment failed.

But that assumes research is somehow outside the process of automation. If AI can write code, design experiments, and interpret results, then a lot of research becomes accessible to it too. The harder question is whether it can choose useful problems and make progress with very little human guidance. My intuition was that those abilities would come last, but I don’t think being the person who builds AI gives you any special protection.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could perform research tasks and raises the challenge of choosing useful problems with little human guidance, but it does not state that AI would become uncontrollable.
